meta.titre: Economic Growth and Development: from rising output to better lives
meta.sous_theme: Growth versus development, how each is measured and when growth improves lives

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Citizenship Education past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Cameroon sells products such as cocoa, coffee, timber and oil to other countries, and the value of what the country produces can rise from one year to the next. Yet a rise in output does not always mean that the farmer in the village or the family in the city lives better. The GCE often asks you to separate economic growth from economic development and to say when the first leads to the second. This lesson gives you the definitions, the measures and the conditions you need.

items: Goods are things we can touch, such as bread, and services are activities done for others, such as teaching.
Output, or production, is the total amount of goods and services produced.
The standard of living describes how well people live: food, housing, health, education and income.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Economic growth
Economic growth is a sustained increase in a country's output of goods and services over time. It is measured by the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which is the total value of the goods and services produced in a country in one year. The rate of growth is found with

$\text{growth rate} = \frac{\text{new GDP} - \text{old GDP}}{\text{old GDP}} \times 100\%$

and GDP per capita is $\frac{\text{GDP}}{\text{population}}$, the average output per person.

### Economic development
Economic development is the improvement in the standard of living and well-being of the people: higher real incomes, less poverty, better health care and education, clean water, more jobs and a fairer sharing of income. Besides GDP per capita, it is judged by life expectancy, literacy rate and infant death rate. The Human Development Index (HDI) of the United Nations combines income, health and education in one figure.

| | Economic growth | Economic development |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | A rise in the output of goods and services | An improvement in the quality of life of the people |
| Nature | Mainly about quantity and money | Quantity and quality, including social change |
| Measures | GDP and its growth rate | HDI, literacy, life expectancy, poverty level |
| Relation | Can happen without development | Usually needs growth, but growth alone is not enough |

### When does growth lead to development?
Growth brings development when the benefits reach ordinary people. This needs fair sharing of income, public spending on schools, hospitals, roads and water, honest management of public money, peace and political stability, protection of the environment, fair taxes whose revenue is used for services, and a population that grows more slowly than output.

### Factors of growth and obstacles
Growth depends on natural resources, labour, capital such as machines and money, technology, enterprising people and good infrastructure. Obstacles include corruption, poor roads and electricity, low skills, war, heavy debt, dependence on a few raw materials and natural disasters.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When both words appear in one question
variantes.contenu_markdown: Define each in one sentence, then give at least two differences from a table: quantity or quality, the measure used, and whether the people's lives change. Add a short example, such as a country whose output rises while most people stay poor.

variantes.nom: Conditions for growth to lead to development
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks which conditions are or are not necessary
variantes.contenu_markdown: Test every statement with one question: does it help the benefits of growth to reach ordinary people, or does it have nothing to do with them? Fair sharing, honest government, spending on education and health, and peace pass the test.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When figures for GDP and population are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Write the formula first, replace the numbers, then give the unit or the percentage sign. Compare GDP per capita over two years before saying whether people on average are better off.

sections.enonce_markdown: In an invented country, GDP is 2,000 billion FCFA in year 1 and 2,100 billion FCFA in year 2. The population is 20 million in year 1 and 21 million in year 2. (a) Calculate the growth rate of GDP. (b) Calculate GDP per capita in each year. (c) Does the growth show an improvement in the average standard of living? Explain.

etapes.action: Write the formula for the growth rate.
etapes.justification: A rate compares the change with the starting value.
The change is 100 billion FCFA, which is divided by 2,000 billion.

etapes.action: Calculate GDP per capita in year 1.
Calculate GDP per capita in year 2.
etapes.justification: The same formula is used with the new data.
The average person is better off only if output per person rises.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Output grew by 5% but the population also grew by 5%, so output per person did not change.

sections.conclusion_markdown:
(a) The growth rate of GDP is 5%.

(b) GDP per capita is 100,000 FCFA in year 1 and 100,000 FCFA in year 2.

(c) No. Although output rose by 5%, the population rose by the same percentage, so the output per person stayed the same. There is growth, but there is no improvement in the average standard of living, and so no sign yet of development.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'Economic growth and economic development mean the same thing.'
items.pourquoi_faux: Growth is a rise in output. Development is a wider improvement in people's lives and may include health, education and fairness.
items.correction_markdown: Growth is an increase in the output of goods and services; development is an improvement in the standard of living and well-being of the people.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'GDP is the money kept in the treasury of the government.'
items.pourquoi_faux: GDP measures production in the whole country, not the savings of the government.
items.correction_markdown: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year.

items.erreur_markdown: A student calculates the growth rate as 'new GDP minus old GDP'.
items.pourquoi_faux: This gives the change in amount only. A rate compares the change with the old value and is expressed as a percentage.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'If GDP per capita is high, everyone in the country lives well.'
items.pourquoi_faux: GDP per capita is an average. Income can still be shared very unfairly, so many people may remain poor.
items.correction_markdown: A high average does not prove development. Look also at the sharing of income, health and education.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'GDP per capita is the GDP of a region.'
items.pourquoi_faux: 'Per capita' means 'per person': the GDP is divided by the number of people.
items.correction_markdown: GDP per capita is the GDP divided by the population.

items.enonce_markdown: State whether each statement describes economic growth or economic development: (a) the value of the cocoa harvest of a country rises by 8%; (b) fewer babies die because new health centres have opened in villages; (c) more adults can read and write; (d) a factory increases its output of soap.
items.solution_markdown: (a) **Growth**; (b) **development**; (c) **development**; (d) **growth**. Rises in the amount produced are growth, while better health and education show development.

items.enonce_markdown: In an invented country, GDP is 4,500 billion FCFA last year and 4,860 billion FCFA this year. The population is 18 million in both years. (a) Calculate the growth rate. (b) Calculate GDP per capita for each year. (c) By how much did GDP per capita rise?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Growth rate $= \frac{4860 - 4500}{4500} \times 100\% = \frac{360}{4500} \times 100\% = $ **8%**.

(b) Last year: 4,500 billion / 18 million = **250,000 FCFA**. This year: 4,860 billion / 18 million = **270,000 FCFA**.

(c) 270,000 - 250,000 = **20,000 FCFA** per person.

items.enonce_markdown: A country earns large new revenues from selling oil, so its GDP grows fast. Most of the money goes to a small group of people, and little is spent on schools, hospitals or roads. (a) Explain why this growth may not lead to development. (b) State three conditions under which the same growth could improve the lives of most citizens.
items.solution_markdown:
Award marks for developed points.

(a) Development needs the benefits to reach ordinary people. If income stays in a few hands and public services are neglected, most families remain poor, children stay out of school and health care is weak, so living standards do not improve even though GDP rises.

(b) Three conditions: (1) income is shared more fairly, for example through fair taxes and wages; (2) the State spends the revenue honestly on schools, hospitals, roads and water; (3) peace, good management and low corruption protect public money. Other valid conditions: protecting the environment and training workers.

**Growth leads to development only when its benefits are shared.**

items_markdown: Economic growth is a sustained rise in a country's output of goods and services, measured by GDP.
Economic development is a lasting improvement in living standards: income, health, education, and a fair sharing of wealth.
Growth rate $= \frac{\text{new GDP} - \text{old GDP}}{\text{old GDP}} \times 100\%$; GDP per capita $= \frac{\text{GDP}}{\text{population}}$.
Growth can occur without development; development usually needs growth.
Growth leads to development when income is shared fairly, public money is spent honestly on services, and the country is at peace.
Obstacles include corruption, poor infrastructure, low skills, war, heavy debt and dependence on a few raw materials.
